title: Giant Star That Fakes a Supernova Every 113 Days Has a Hidden Black Hole or Neutron Star Partner
byline: Lucas Caldwell Published: Nov 19 2026, 4:09 AM EST
excerpt: A giant star that erupts every 113 days without dying likely has a black hole or neutron star partner, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory finds.
content:
A massive star that has erupted at least 27 times since 2012 without dying appears to have a hidden partner, either a black hole or a neutron star, that triggers its outbursts on a regular cycle, according to a study in The Astrophysical Journal announced by NASA on Nov. 9. The star, called AT 2016blu, brightens roughly every 113 days, or a little more than three times a year.

Each outburst looks enough like an exploding star that astronomers call AT 2016blu a "supernova impostor." Unlike a true supernova, though, the star survives every time. The new X-ray observations offer the first explanation for why the eruptions keep coming on schedule.

The finding matters beyond one star. It identifies a new way that massive stars can lose material and brighten dramatically, and it gives astronomers a way to separate real supernovas from impostors in the flood of data expected from new sky surveys.

The Star That Would Not Die

AT 2016blu sits in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, about 30 million light-years from Earth. It is at least 33 times as massive as the Sun and belongs to a rare class called luminous blue variables, or LBVs, which are hot, extremely bright, and unstable.

LBVs are known for violent eruptions that can briefly make them nearly as bright as a supernova. The most famous example is Eta Carinae in our own galaxy, whose 19th-century eruption was visible to the naked eye. Because massive stars often flare before they explode, astronomers first suspected AT 2016blu might be close to the end of its life.

Its behavior did not fit — the outbursts kept repeating at regular intervals, which no single supernova explosion can do. Co-author Núria Torres-Albà of the University of Virginia said the star was confusing at first because "it kept acting like a supernova."

Chandra Catches the Hidden Partner

Lead author Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia and her colleagues predicted when the next outburst would occur and asked Chandra to interrupt its schedule. Through its Target of Opportunity program, Chandra observed the star from March 24 to 27, 2026, during an optical eruption.

Chandra was the only X-ray telescope sharp enough to separate AT 2016blu from a bright X-ray source nearby. The March data showed the star at least 100 times brighter in X-rays than in Chandra observations from 2001 and 2002, before the outbursts began.

That X-ray glow is the key clue — material falling onto a black hole or neutron star heats up to millions of degrees and shines in X-rays. The team proposes that the compact companion travels on an orbit that brings it close to the giant star roughly every 113 days. Each close pass pulls gas from the star; the captured material heats up, and X-rays from the companion heat the surrounding gas, which then glows brightly in visible light.

The authors describe AT 2016blu as "the first known LBV system with a compact companion," as reported by Universe Today. It is also the first X-ray detection of this kind of erupting star. The system is bright enough in X-rays to be a candidate ultraluminous X-ray source, a poorly understood class of objects.

Open Questions About the Companion

The 113-day rhythm likely reflects the orbit itself, with each outburst marking a close approach. Because AT 2016blu is about 30 million light-years away, the eruptions astronomers see today actually happened about 30 million years ago, long before humans existed.

The study cannot yet say whether the companion is a black hole or a neutron star. Both are the collapsed remains of massive stars. A neutron star packs more than the Sun's mass into a city-sized sphere, while a stellar-mass black hole is so dense that not even light escapes, yet both can pull in gas and emit X-rays in similar ways. Further observations could narrow that down.

It is also unclear whether other supernova impostors work the same way. Space.com reports that only one other impostor has so far shown X-ray emission typical of material being stolen by a compact object. Some LBV eruptions may still come from instabilities inside the star alone.

Nor does the finding settle the star's ultimate fate. A star more than 33 times the Sun's mass will eventually collapse, but the study does not predict when, and the regular outbursts are not a countdown to a supernova.

Amateur Astronomers and Future Surveys

The discovery relied on years of monitoring. Optical observations came from the Katzman Automatic Imaging Telescope, the Las Cumbres Observatory Global Supernova Project and the American Association of Variable Star Observers, including data from more than 30 amateur astronomers. That backyard contribution helped pin down the 113-day rhythm.

Aghakhanloo has additional Chandra time to study other impostors. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory's survey of the southern sky is expected to find many more candidate eruptions, making it more important to tell real supernovas from stars that only appear to explode. X-ray follow-up like the Chandra campaign may become a standard test for sorting them.

For readers, AT 2016blu is too distant to see without large telescopes. Amateur observers interested in contributing to similar research can join variable-star programs such as AAVSO, whose members supplied part of the data behind this finding.

The next milestone will be X-ray observations during future outbursts, which could reveal whether the companion is a black hole or a neutron star and how much material it steals on each pass.

What Readers Want to Know

What is AT 2016blu? A luminous blue variable star at least 33 times the Sun's mass in the galaxy NGC 4559, about 30 million light-years away.

What is a supernova impostor? A star whose outburst looks like a supernova but which survives the eruption instead of being destroyed.

How often does AT 2016blu erupt? About every 113 days. Astronomers have recorded at least 27 outbursts since 2012.

What did Chandra find? During a March 2026 outburst, the star was at least 100 times brighter in X-rays than before the eruptions began, pointing to a compact companion.

Is the companion a black hole or a neutron star? Scientists do not know yet. Either could produce the X-rays seen by Chandra.

Is the star about to explode? The study does not predict a supernova. The regular outbursts are driven by the companion, not a countdown to explosion.
